title: Clothe the naked
tomorrow: Luke's Christmas story: where exactly is the innkeeper?

cards: A hoodie tossed to a friend shivering in the bleachers at a night game says more than "here." It says, you're not out in the cold alone. Now winter, at a city gate, long ago.
A young soldier named Martin meets a man by the road with almost nothing on. Martin has already given away everything else. All that's left is his military cloak.
So he draws his sword, cuts it in two, and hands half down. A few people watching laugh at how he looks in what's left.

teach.b: Why cover someone? Martin's story, told by Sulpicius Severus, answers it that night. Martin dreams of Christ wearing the half cloak, telling the angels that Martin, not yet baptized, clothed him with it.
That's Matthew 25 come to life. In the Douay-Rheims the king says, "Naked, and you covered me." And notice the word half.
The story doesn't ask Martin to freeze. He shared what he was wearing. A neighbor tradition asks the same question and finds its answer in the first pages of the Bible.

After Adam and Eve leave the garden, in the Jewish Publication Society's translation: "And the LORD God made for Adam and for his wife garments of skins, and clothed them." The Talmud reads that as a pattern.

teach.h: AS GOD CLOTHES, SO YOU CLOTHE.
teach.b: Walk in God's ways, the rabbis teach: as God clothes the naked, so you clothe the naked. Jews and Catholics both treat clothing a person as holy work, not just kindness.
The difference is honest, and it's in where each looks.
Catholics, with Matthew, see Christ in the one being covered.
The Talmud sees the giver imitating the God who covered first. And both stories hear more than warmth. Clothes let a person walk into a room without shame.

how: Catholics clothe the naked through parish coat drives, clothing closets and shelters, and Saint Martin of Tours, who shared his cloak, is remembered as a patron of this work.

o: give clothes to someone in need, and keep their dignity
make sure every saint's statue is properly robed
dress modestly so that you never draw attention

he cut it in two and shared half.

games.q: walking home from a late game, your friend is freezing and you have one jacket and a hoodie under it. what does Martin's story suggest?
o: give her everything and walk home cold yourself.
share what you have: hand over the jacket, keep the hoodie.
keep both; you can't give what you need yourself.
games.why: Martin cut his cloak in two and shared half. the story doesn't ask him to freeze; it asks him to share what he's wearing.

practice: Go to the closet or drawer nearest you, or call it to mind, and look at one coat or sweater you no longer wear. Hold it, feel its weight, and see it on someone who'll be cold tonight.
If you pray, rest on the king's words: naked, and you covered me.

wordCard.voice: Clothe the naked. Cover someone who lacks clothes, the way Martin did with half a cloak.

orig.note: Greek, naked: the word in Matthew 25:36, naked, and you covered me.

carryVoice: Here's the line: clothe him, because in Martin's dream the stranger's half cloak was on Christ. Take care.
